faq.answer: No. Pay, authority, safety, recognition of existing work, or limited career options may explain promotion seeking. Compare equal contributions under different titles and audiences.
faq.question: Does seeking promotion establish Social Type Three?

faq.answer: Changing title while holding contribution closer helps reveal whether rank itself changes attention. Sponsorship, power, and real compensation differences must still be recorded.
faq.question: Why rotate title in the comparison?

faq.answer: Stable private contribution without credit, challenging a group standard despite status loss, or rank concern confined to a promotion window would weaken it.
faq.question: What weakens the social-subtype hypothesis?

sections.body_md: The traditional description proposes that Type Three result attention may track position, contribution, and what a group recognizes. It does not establish a social cause or make hierarchy a permanent trait.
sections.title: Treat rank attention as a traditional hypothesis

sections.body_md: Compare equal contributions under a named leadership title, anonymous collaboration, and public representation. Record effort, credit claims, standard-setting, and response when the title rotates to another person.
sections.title: Match contribution while changing title and audience

sections.body_md: Social subtype language organizes observations about audience, rank, and group standards. It is not evidence about bodily mechanisms, a universal hierarchy drive, or a category that determines conduct.
sections.title: Keep social language observational

sections.body_md: A person may frame ambition as protecting the team's reputation or meeting a shared standard. That less self-advertising variation still requires comparison with genuine duty, solidarity, and institutional accountability.
sections.title: Allow service to the group to mask visibility

sections.body_md: Formal hierarchy, representation duty, sponsorship, discrimination, scarce promotion slots, and public accountability change how rank is handled. Record who can refuse visibility and who bears the cost of being overlooked.
sections.title: Test promotion rules and unequal power

sections.body_md: The hypothesis weakens when contribution remains unchanged after title and credit disappear, group standards are challenged despite status cost, or rank concern appears only during a formal promotion cycle.
sections.title: Use rotating status and private contribution as tests

sections.body_md: Instrument-specific findings do not establish universal subtypes. This page cannot predict leadership, promotion, influence, group loyalty, employability, or social value.
sections.title: Keep rank observations non-predictive

sections.body_md:
Duration: 5

Context: Choose one named leadership task, one anonymous group contribution, and one situation where a title rotates.

Observable signal: Record contribution, decision authority, audience, credit, compensation, group standard, refusal cost, and behavior after rotation.

Page-specific signal: Compare whether the same work changes meaning when rank and public recognition change.

Alternative explanation: Compare promotion rules, representation duty, sponsorship, discrimination, solidarity, and unequal power.

Reflection prompt: Identify the event where institutional incentives explain rank attention better than subtype.

seo.description: Social Type Three is a traditional, evidence-limited hypothesis that achievement attention may be expressed through rank, recognized contribution, and the standards of a valued group. Public leadership cannot establish subtype because hierarchy, promotion rules, representation duties, and unequal power can produce the same behavior.
seo.title: Social Type Three: rank and group standards as a matched-comparison hypothesis
